items.stem: What is the Avogadro constant?
items.answer: 6.02 × 10²³ particles per mole
items.markingKey: One mole of any substance contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles.

items.stem: Explain why 1 mol of hydrogen gas, H₂, has a mass of 2 g but 1 mol of hydrogen atoms has a mass of 1 g.
items.answer: Each H₂ molecule contains two H atoms, so Mr(H₂) = 2; 1 mol of molecules contains 2 mol of atoms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: H₂ diatomic Mr = 2; 1 mark: 2 mol atoms per mol molecules [2]

items.stem: Explain why 10 g of magnesium contains more atoms than 10 g of copper.
items.answer: Magnesium atoms are lighter (Ar 24 vs 64), so 10 g contains more moles (0.417 vs 0.156 mol) and therefore more atoms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Ar comparison; 1 mark: more moles → more atoms [2]

items.stem: Calculate the mass of 0.600 mol of potassium hydroxide, KOH. (Ar: H = 1, K = 39, O = 16)
Calculate the number of formula units in 39.6 g of ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄. (Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ /mol) (Ar: H = 1, N = 14, O = 16, S = 32)
Calculate the number of O atoms in 21.6 g of water, H₂O. (Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ /mol) (Ar: H = 1, O = 16)

Yusuf weighs 120 g of ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, on a balance in a quality-control laboratory. (Ar: H = 1, N = 14, O = 16) (Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ /mol) (a) Calculate the relative formula mass of NH₄NO₃. (b) Calculate the number of moles in the sample. (c) Calculate the percentage by mass of H in NH₄NO₃.

A sample of sulfur trioxide, SO₃, has a mass of 1.60 g. (Ar: O = 16, S = 32) (Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ /mol) (a) Calculate the relative formula mass of SO₃. (b) Calculate the number of moles of O atoms in the sample. (c) Calculate the percentage by mass of O in SO₃. (d) Calculate the mass of SO₃ that would contain twice as many particles as this sample.
Which quantity has the unit mol?
items.answer: amount of substance
items.markingKey: The mole is the unit of amount of substance.

items.stem: Which contains the greatest number of atoms?
items.answer: 1 mol of methane, CH₄
items.markingKey: CH₄: 5 atoms per molecule → 5 mol atoms.

items.stem: A student calculates the number of moles in 32 g of oxygen gas as 2 mol. Explain the error.
items.answer: Oxygen gas is O₂ with Mr 32, so 32 g is 1 mol of O₂ molecules; the student used Ar (16) instead of Mr.

items.stem: Explain what is meant by "one mole" of a substance.
items.answer: The amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles (atoms, molecules or ions) – the Avogadro constant; its mass in grams equals the Ar or Mr.

items.stem: Calculate the mass of 0.800 mol of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃. (Ar: C = 12, Na = 23, O = 16)
What is meant by the limiting reactant?
options: the reactant left over at the end
the catalyst used in the reaction
the reactant present in the greatest mass
the reactant that is completely used up and so limits the amount of product
items.answer: the reactant that is completely used up and so limits the amount of product
items.markingKey: Limiting reactant runs out first; the other is in excess.

items.stem: Explain why adding more of the reactant that is in excess does not increase the mass of product.
items.answer: The amount of product depends on the limiting reactant; once it has all reacted, extra excess reactant has nothing to react with.

items.stem: Explain how you would use a balanced equation to find the mass of product from a known mass of reactant.
items.answer: Convert mass of reactant to moles (÷ Mr); use the mole ratio from the equation to find moles of product; multiply by Mr of product.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: moles of reactant; 1 mark: mole ratio; 1 mark: × Mr of product [3]

items.stem: Priya reacts 16.0 g of H₂O completely. 2Li + 2H₂O → 2LiOH + H₂. Calculate the mass of H₂ formed. (Ar: H = 1, O = 16)
Felix reacts 4.00 g of H₂O completely. 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Calculate the mass of H₂ formed. (Ar: H = 1, O = 16)
Use the equation 2Mg + CO₂ → 2MgO + C to calculate the maximum mass of MgO that can be made from 12.0 g of CO₂. (Ar: C = 12, Mg = 24, O = 16)

A manufacturer in Manila makes MgO by the reaction magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide, starting from 2.40 g of Mg. 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16) (a) Calculate the number of moles of Mg used. (b) The actual mass obtained was 3.00 g. Calculate the percentage yield. (c) Suggest two reasons why the percentage yield is less than 100%.
items.answer: (a) 0.100 mol (b) 75.0% (c) product lost on transfer/filtration; reaction incomplete; side reactions; impure reactant

items.stem: A manufacturer in Kuala Lumpur makes H₂O by the reaction methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, starting from 12.0 g of O₂. CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (Ar: H = 1, O = 16) (a) Deduce the number of moles of H₂O that can form. (b) Calculate the theoretical (maximum) mass of H₂O. (c) The actual mass obtained was 5.74 g. Calculate the percentage yield. (d) Suggest two reasons why the percentage yield is less than 100%.
items.answer: (a) 0.375 mol (b) 6.75 g (c) 85.0% (d) product lost on transfer/filtration; reaction incomplete; side reactions; impure reactant

items.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 20 g and an actual yield of 15 g. What is the percentage yield?
A student obtains a percentage yield of 108% for a dried precipitate. Suggest a reason for this.
items.answer: The product was not completely dry (still contained water) or was contaminated with another substance.

items.stem: Explain why a reversible reaction cannot have a 100% yield.
items.answer: The products re-form the reactants, so at equilibrium not all reactants have been converted to products.

items.stem: In a factory in Colombo, 50.0 g of H₂O react in the reaction Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂. Calculate the mass of H₂ produced. (Ar: H = 1, O = 16)
13.8 g of Na is mixed with 26.6 g of Cl₂. 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl. Deduce which reactant is limiting and calculate the mass of NaCl formed. (Ar: Cl = 35.5, Na = 23)
items.answer: Na is limiting; 35.1 g of NaCl
items.markingKey: n(Na) = 0.600 mol, n(Cl₂) = 0.375 mol [1]; compare with ratio 2:1 → Na limiting, Cl₂ in excess [1]; n(NaCl) = 0.600 mol [1]; mass = 0.600 × 58.5 = 35.1 g [1]

items.stem: What is the volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure?
items.answer: 24 dm³
items.markingKey: Molar gas volume at r.t.p. = 24 dm³ (24 000 cm³).

items.stem: Explain why 1 mol of hydrogen and 1 mol of carbon dioxide occupy the same volume at r.t.p.
items.answer: In a gas the particles are very far apart, so the volume depends on the number of particles, not their size or mass; equal moles → equal volumes.

items.stem: Explain how to convert a concentration in mol/dm³ to g/dm³.
items.answer: Multiply the concentration in mol/dm³ by the molar mass (Mr) of the solute.

items.stem: Calculate the volume at r.t.p. occupied by 29.0 g of butane, C₄H₁₀. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)
items.answer: 12.0 dm³

items.stem: Calculate the volume at r.t.p. occupied by 1.16 g of butane, C₄H₁₀. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)

Aisha adds 5.85 g of Zn to 40.0 cm³ of 1.50 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid. Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂ (Ar: Zn = 65) (a) Calculate the number of moles of acid used. (b) Deduce which reactant is in excess. (c) Calculate the concentration of the acid in g/dm³. (d) Describe how the volume of H₂ could be measured.
items.answer: (a) 0.0600 mol (b) Zn (c) 147 g/dm³ (d) collect in a gas syringe (or over water in an inverted measuring cylinder)

items.stem: A student calculates the moles in 25 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ acid as 2.5 mol. Explain the error.
items.answer: The volume must be in dm³: 25 cm³ = 0.025 dm³, so moles = 0.025 × 0.1 = 0.0025 mol.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: volume not converted to dm³; 1 mark: 0.0025 mol [2]

items.stem: Grace uses 0.120 g of MgCO₃: magnesium carbonate reacts with excess hydrochloric acid. MgCO₃ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the volume of CO₂ produced at r.t.p., in cm³. (Ar: C = 12, Mg = 24, O = 16)
items.answer: 34.3 cm³

items.stem: Calculate the volume at r.t.p. occupied by 4.20 g of nitrogen, N₂. (Ar: N = 14)
items.answer: 3.60 dm³

items.stem: Yusuf adds 0.338 g of Al to 25.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂ (Ar: Al = 27) (a) Deduce which reactant is in excess. (b) Calculate the maximum volume of H₂ produced at r.t.p., in cm³. (c) Calculate the concentration of the acid in g/dm³.
items.answer: (a) Al (b) 150 cm³ (c) 18.3 g/dm³

items.stem: What is an empirical formula?
options: the actual number of atoms in one molecule
the formula of the ions in a compound
the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound
items.answer: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound

items.stem: Explain why the empirical formula of an ionic compound is the same as the formula normally written for it.
items.answer: An ionic compound is a giant lattice, not discrete molecules; its formula already shows the simplest ratio of ions.

items.stem: Explain why the empirical formula alone is not enough to identify a molecular compound.
items.answer: Different compounds can share the same empirical formula (e.g. C₂H₄ and C₃H₆ are both CH₂); the Mr is needed to find the molecular formula.

items.stem: Analysis of 3.00 g of a compound shows that it contains 0.91 g of N, 2.09 g of O. Calculate the empirical formula of the compound. (Ar: N = 14, O = 16)
items.answer: NO₂
items.markingKey: moles: N 0.0652, O 0.130 [1]; divide by smallest: N 1.00, O 2.00 [1]; empirical formula NO₂ [1]

items.stem: Analysis of 5.00 g of a compound shows that it contains 4.29 g of C, 0.71 g of H. Calculate the empirical formula of the compound. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)
items.answer: CH₂
items.markingKey: moles: C 0.357, H 0.714 [1]; divide by smallest: C 1.00, H 2.00 [1]; empirical formula CH₂ [1]

items.stem: Diego heats zinc in a crucible to find the formula of its oxide. Results: mass of crucible + lid = 18.42 g; mass of crucible + lid + zinc = 19.39 g; mass of crucible + lid + oxide after heating to constant mass = 19.63 g. (Ar: O = 16, Zn = 65) (a) Calculate the empirical formula of the oxide. (b) Explain why the lid is lifted occasionally during heating.
items.answer: (a) ZnO (b) to let in air (oxygen) for the reaction while minimising loss of product

items.stem: Explain why a lid is lifted from time to time when magnesium is heated in a crucible to find the formula of magnesium oxide.
items.answer: To let oxygen in so that all the magnesium reacts, while keeping the lid on most of the time stops magnesium oxide smoke escaping.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: let oxygen in; 1 mark: prevent loss of product [2]

items.stem: Calculate the percentage by mass of O in sulfur dioxide, SO₂. (Ar: O = 16, S = 32)

Isla heats magnesium in a crucible to find the formula of its oxide. Results: mass of crucible + lid = 19.88 g; mass of crucible + lid + magnesium = 21.08 g; mass of crucible + lid + oxide after heating to constant mass = 21.88 g. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16) (a) Explain why the crucible is heated to constant mass. (b) Calculate the percentage by mass of Mg in the oxide. (c) Explain why the lid is lifted occasionally during heating.
items.answer: (a) to make sure all the metal has reacted (b) 60.0% (c) to let in air (oxygen) for the reaction while minimising loss of product

items.stem: Noah heats copper in a crucible to find the formula of its oxide. Results: mass of crucible + lid = 21.04 g; mass of crucible + lid + copper = 22.32 g; mass of crucible + lid + oxide after heating to constant mass = 22.64 g. (Ar: Cu = 64, O = 16) (a) Calculate the mass of copper used and the mass of oxygen that combined with it. (b) Calculate the empirical formula of the oxide. (c) Explain why the lid is lifted occasionally during heating.
items.answer: (a) 1.28 g; 0.32 g (b) CuO (c) to let in air (oxygen) for the reaction while minimising loss of product

items.stem: What is meant by concordant titres?
options: titres that agree within 0.10 cm³ of each other
titres that are exactly the same as the rough titre
titres within 1.0 cm³ of each other
items.answer: titres that agree within 0.10 cm³ of each other
items.markingKey: Concordant results are within 0.10 cm³; only these are averaged.

items.stem: Explain why the conical flask is swirled during a titration.
items.answer: To mix the solutions so the acid and alkali react completely and the colour change at the end-point is seen accurately.

items.stem: Explain why a white tile is placed under the conical flask.
items.answer: It makes the colour change of the indicator easier to see, so the end-point is judged accurately.

items.stem: Titration results (cm³): rough 35.90, 34.80, 34.85, 34.90. Identify the concordant titres and calculate the mean titre, giving your answer to 2 decimal places.
items.answer: concordant: 34.80, 34.85, 34.90; mean 34.85 cm³

items.stem: Sofia titrates 20.0 cm³ of potassium hydroxide solution of unknown concentration with 0.200 mol/dm³ nitric acid, using methyl orange indicator. Titres (cm³): rough 20.60; titre 1: 19.95; titre 2: 20.00; titre 3: 20.00. KOH + HNO₃ → KNO₃ + H₂O Identify the concordant titres and calculate the mean titre. Calculate the concentration of the potassium hydroxide in mol/dm³.
items.answer: mean titre 19.98 cm³; concentration 0.200 mol/dm³

items.stem: Lucas carries out a titration to find the concentration of a solution of sodium hydroxide. 25.0 cm³ of the sodium hydroxide is titrated with 0.200 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. Titres (cm³): rough 15.50, 15.45, 15.05, 15.00. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O (a) Name the apparatus used to measure the 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide and the apparatus used to add the acid. (b) Calculate the mean of the concordant titres. (c) Explain why the titration is repeated until concordant results are obtained.
items.answer: (a) volumetric pipette; burette (b) 15.03 cm³ (c) to check reliability / identify and discard anomalous results

items.stem: Explain why the solution is added drop by drop near the end-point.
items.answer: So that the end-point is not overshot; one drop can change the indicator colour.

items.stem: Calculate the volume of 0.0800 mol/dm³ nitric acid needed to neutralise 20.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide. NaOH + HNO₃ → NaNO₃ + H₂O
items.answer: 50.0 cm³

items.stem: Noah carries out a titration to find the concentration of a solution of potassium hydroxide. 25.0 cm³ of the potassium hydroxide is titrated with 0.0500 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid. Titres (cm³): rough 26.20, 24.95, 25.00, 25.30. 2KOH + H₂SO₄ → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O (a) Name the apparatus used to measure the 25.0 cm³ of potassium hydroxide and the apparatus used to add the acid. (b) Suggest a suitable indicator and give the colour change at the end-point. (c) Calculate the mean of the concordant titres. (d) Explain why the titration is repeated until concordant results are obtained.
items.answer: (a) volumetric pipette; burette (b) methyl orange: yellow to orange (or thymolphthalein: blue to colourless) (c) 24.98 cm³ (d) to check reliability / identify and discard anomalous results
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark indicator; 1 mark colours [2] (c) concordant only [1] (d) [1]

items.stem: What is the mass of one mole of oxygen molecules, O₂? (Ar: O = 16)
Explain why relative formula mass has no units.
items.answer: It is a ratio: the mass of a formula unit compared with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

items.stem: Calculate the mass of 0.600 mol of sodium chloride, NaCl. (Ar: Cl = 35.5, Na = 23)
Isla weighs out 2.84 g of sodium sulfate, Na₂SO₄. Calculate the number of moles of sodium sulfate. (Ar: Na = 23, O = 16, S = 32)

A sample of zinc oxide, ZnO, has a mass of 48.6 g. (Ar: O = 16, Zn = 65) (Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ /mol) (a) Calculate the number of moles in the sample. (b) Calculate the number of moles of Zn atoms in the sample. (c) Calculate the number of formula units in the sample. (d) Calculate the mass of ZnO that would contain twice as many particles as this sample.
Why is the actual yield of a reaction usually less than the theoretical yield?
options: Some product is lost during separation or the reaction does not go to completion.
Mass is destroyed in the reaction.
The limiting reactant is in excess.
items.answer: Some product is lost during separation or the reaction does not go to completion.
items.markingKey: Losses on filtering/transfer, side reactions, incomplete or reversible reactions.

items.stem: Grace calculates the mass of H₂O made from 6.00 g of O₂ in the reaction 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O and gets 3.38 g. Identify the error and give the correct answer. (Ar: H = 1, O = 16)
items.answer: The mole ratio 7:6 from the equation was ignored. Correct: n = 0.188 mol O₂ → 0.161 mol H₂O → 2.89 g.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: mole ratio not used; 1 mark: correct answer 2.89 g [2]

items.stem: The theoretical yield of Fe in a reaction is 24.9 g. Kenji obtains 19.4 g. Calculate the percentage yield.

Amara carries out the reaction ethanol + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water using 40.0 g of O₂. C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O (Ar: C = 12, O = 16) (a) Calculate the number of moles of O₂ used. (b) The actual mass obtained was 29.3 g. Calculate the percentage yield. (c) Suggest two reasons why the percentage yield is less than 100%.
items.answer: (a) 1.25 mol (b) 79.8% (c) product lost on transfer/filtration; reaction incomplete; side reactions; impure reactant

items.stem: Jonas carries out the reaction calcium oxide + water → calcium hydroxide using 20.0 g of CaO. CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ (Ar: Ca = 40, H = 1, O = 16) (a) Deduce the number of moles of Ca(OH)₂ that can form. (b) The actual mass obtained was 18.5 g. Calculate the percentage yield. (c) Suggest two reasons why the percentage yield is less than 100%. (d) Calculate the mass of CaO needed to make 52.9 g of Ca(OH)₂ at 100% yield.
items.answer: (a) 0.357 mol (b) 70.1% (c) product lost on transfer/filtration; reaction incomplete; side reactions; impure reactant (d) 40.0 g
items.markingKey: (a) ratio 1:1 [1] (b) 18.5 ÷ 26.4 × 100 [1] (c) 1 mark each [2] (d) double the quantities [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is the volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure? (b) What volume is occupied by 0.5 mol of carbon dioxide at r.t.p.?
items.answer: (a) 24 dm³ (b) 12 dm³
items.markingKey: (a) Molar gas volume at r.t.p. = 24 dm³ (24 000 cm³). (b) 0.5 × 24 = 12 dm³.

items.stem: Explain why the molar gas volume of 24 dm³ applies only at room temperature and pressure.
items.answer: Gas volume depends on temperature and pressure; at a higher temperature or lower pressure the same number of moles occupies a larger volume.

items.stem: Convert a concentration of 0.0500 mol/dm³ of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, into g/dm³. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
items.answer: 9.00 g/dm³

items.stem: Ethan adds 4.73 g of MgCO₃ to 50.0 cm³ of 1.50 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. MgCO₃ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂ (Ar: C = 12, Mg = 24, O = 16) (a) Calculate the number of moles of MgCO₃ added. (b) Deduce which reactant is in excess. (c) Calculate the maximum volume of CO₂ produced at r.t.p., in cm³. (d) Calculate the concentration of the acid in g/dm³. (e) Describe how the volume of CO₂ could be measured.
items.answer: (a) 0.0563 mol (b) MgCO₃ (c) 900 cm³ (d) 54.8 g/dm³ (e) collect in a gas syringe (or over water in an inverted measuring cylinder)

items.stem: Explain why it is important for medicines to have a high percentage purity.
items.answer: Impurities could be harmful or reduce the effectiveness/dose of the active substance.

items.stem: Compound Z has the empirical formula CH₂ and a relative molecular mass of 28. Explain how to deduce its molecular formula and state the molecular formula. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)
items.answer: Mr of CH₂ = 14; 28 ÷ 14 = 2; multiply the empirical formula by 2: C₂H₄.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Mr of empirical formula 14; 1 mark: ratio 2; 1 mark: C₂H₄ [3]

items.stem: A compound has the following composition by mass: C 84.2%, H 15.8%. Calculate its empirical formula. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)
items.answer: C₄H₉
items.markingKey: moles: C 7.02, H 15.8 [1]; divide by smallest: C 1.00, H 2.25 (× 4) [1]; empirical formula C₄H₉ [1]

items.stem: A student does not rinse the burette with acid but leaves it wet with water. Explain the effect on the titre.
items.answer: The acid is diluted, so more acid is needed to neutralise the alkali – the titre is too large and the calculated alkali concentration too high.

items.stem: Lucas titrates 20.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution of unknown concentration with 0.150 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid, using thymolphthalein indicator. Titres (cm³): rough 27.20; titre 1: 26.60; titre 2: 26.65; titre 3: 26.30. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O Identify the concordant titres and calculate the mean titre. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide in mol/dm³.
items.answer: mean titre 26.62 cm³; concentration 0.200 mol/dm³

items.stem: Titration results (cm³): rough 31.60, 30.55, 30.20, 30.60. Identify the concordant titres and calculate the mean titre, giving your answer to 2 decimal places. Explain why the rough titre is excluded.
items.answer: concordant: 30.55, 30.60; mean 30.58 cm³; the rough titre is only approximate (end-point overshot).

items.stem: Define relative formula mass, Mr.
items.answer: The sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms shown in the formula.

items.stem: Sofia says that 48.0 g of lead and 48.0 g of calcium must contain the same number of atoms because they have the same mass. Explain why this is incorrect. (Ar: Pb = 207, Ca = 40)
items.answer: The atoms have different masses, so equal masses contain different numbers of moles: lead 0.232 mol, calcium 1.20 mol; calcium has more atoms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: atoms of different elements have different masses; 1 mark: moles calculated / compared; total [2]

items.stem: Calculate the number of formula units in 20.4 g of aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃. (Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ /mol) (Ar: Al = 27, O = 16)
Calculate the number of formula units in 48.0 g of iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃. (Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ /mol) (Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16)

A sample of aluminium sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃, has a mass of 103 g. (Ar: Al = 27, O = 16, S = 32) (Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ /mol) (a) Calculate the relative formula mass of Al₂(SO₄)₃. (b) Calculate the number of moles in the sample. (c) Calculate the mass of O in the sample. (d) Calculate the mass of Al₂(SO₄)₃ that would contain twice as many particles as this sample.
In the reaction 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, what is the mole ratio of magnesium to magnesium oxide?
Chloe calculates the mass of H₂ made from 10.0 g of K in the reaction 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂ and gets 0.513 g. Identify the error and give the correct answer. (Ar: H = 1, K = 39)
items.answer: The mole ratio 2:1 from the equation was ignored. Correct: n = 0.256 mol K → 0.128 mol H₂ → 0.256 g.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: mole ratio not used; 1 mark: correct answer 0.256 g [2]

items.stem: The theoretical yield of H₂ in a reaction is 0.667 g. Lucas obtains 0.620 g. Calculate the percentage yield.

A manufacturer in Seoul makes CO₂ by the reaction calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide, starting from 4.80 g of CaCO₃. CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (Ar: C = 12, Ca = 40, O = 16) (a) Calculate the number of moles of CaCO₃ used. (b) Deduce the number of moles of CO₂ that can form. (c) The actual mass obtained was 1.58 g. Calculate the percentage yield. (d) Calculate the mass of CaCO₃ needed to make 4.22 g of CO₂ at 100% yield.

A manufacturer in Auckland makes CO₂ by the reaction propane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, starting from 10.0 g of O₂. C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O (Ar: C = 12, O = 16) (a) Calculate the theoretical (maximum) mass of CO₂. (b) The actual mass obtained was 6.19 g. Calculate the percentage yield. (c) Suggest two reasons why the percentage yield is less than 100%. (d) Calculate the mass of O₂ needed to make 16.5 g of CO₂ at 100% yield.
items.answer: (a) 8.25 g (b) 75.0% (c) product lost on transfer/filtration; reaction incomplete; side reactions; impure reactant (d) 20.0 g

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What volume is occupied by 0.5 mol of carbon dioxide at r.t.p.? (b) How many cm³ are there in 1 dm³?
Chloe calculates the moles of sodium hydroxide in 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ solution as 2.00 mol. Explain the error and give the correct answer.
items.answer: The volume was not converted to dm³; n = 0.100 × 20.0/1000 = 0.00200 mol.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: error identified; 1 mark: correct value [2]

items.stem: Use the equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O to calculate the volume of O₂ that reacts with or is produced from 40 cm³ of H₂. All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure.
items.answer: 20.0 cm³
items.markingKey: equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of moles [1]; ratio 2:1 → 40 × 1/2 = 20.0 cm³ [1]

items.stem: Ines adds 7.80 g of Zn to 40.0 cm³ of 1.50 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid. Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂ (Ar: Zn = 65) (a) Calculate the number of moles of acid used. (b) Calculate the number of moles of Zn added. (c) Calculate the maximum volume of H₂ produced at r.t.p., in cm³. (d) Calculate the concentration of the acid in g/dm³. (e) Describe how the volume of H₂ could be measured.
items.answer: (a) 0.0600 mol (b) 0.120 mol (c) 1440 cm³ (d) 147 g/dm³ (e) collect in a gas syringe (or over water in an inverted measuring cylinder)

items.stem: Compound Z has the empirical formula CH and a relative molecular mass of 78. Explain how to deduce its molecular formula and state the molecular formula. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)
items.answer: Mr of CH = 13; 78 ÷ 13 = 6; multiply the empirical formula by 6: C₆H₆.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: method (divide Mr by empirical Mr); 1 mark: C₆H₆ [2]

items.stem: Compound Z has the empirical formula CH₂O and a relative molecular mass of 60. Explain how to deduce its molecular formula and state the molecular formula. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
items.answer: Mr of CH₂O = 30; 60 ÷ 30 = 2; multiply the empirical formula by 2: C₂H₄O₂.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Mr of empirical formula 30; 1 mark: ratio 2; 1 mark: C₂H₄O₂ [3]

items.stem: Analysis of 3.00 g of a compound shows that it contains 1.8 g of Mg, 1.2 g of O. Calculate the empirical formula of the compound. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16)
items.answer: MgO
items.markingKey: moles: Mg 0.0750, O 0.0750 [1]; divide by smallest: Mg 1.00, O 1.00 [1]; empirical formula MgO [1]

items.stem: During a titration, Grace rinses the conical flask with the alkali before adding the pipetted volume. Explain the effect on the results and how the procedure should be improved.
items.answer: Extra alkali stays in the flask, so the titre is too large; rinse the flask with distilled water only.

items.stem: Titration results (cm³): rough 29.60, 29.00, 29.00, 29.10. Identify the concordant titres and calculate the mean titre, giving your answer to 2 decimal places.
items.answer: concordant: 29.00, 29.00, 29.10; mean 29.03 cm³

items.stem: Calculate the volume of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid needed to neutralise 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium carbonate. Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂
items.answer: 40.0 cm³
